articles.title: Read The Room, Skadden — See Also
articles.content:
Bait And Switch: Skadden sent a firmwide email about how well it’s doing financially… and then DIDN’T announce raises or bonuses.

The White House Said Replacing Its Texas Judge Pick Was ‘Impossible,’ Now It’s Vetting The Replacement: Funny how that works when stuffing the bench with conservatives is on the line.

Reeling In Raises: Fish & Richardson associates will see more money in their accounts soon.

Fresh Stacks: Freshfields announced its own match.

Didn’t Get The Memo? Ashurst Perkins Coie is handing out Milbank’s special bonuses now that Cravath has raised the bar.

Raises Are Great, But The Bonus Dough Is Missing: Hopefully Pillsbury will get around to announcing those soon.

articles.title: The Cynical Origin Of The Presidential Turkey Pardon
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

The presidential turkey “pardon” is now a wholesome Thanksgiving photo op — but the word “pardon” entered the ritual almost by accident, as a president’s wisecrack to dodge reporters pressing him about whether he’d grant real pardons to the figures at the center of a major criminal scandal. Which scandal prompted the very first turkey “pardon” quip?

Hint: Reporters wanted to know whether the president in question would spare two of his own officials — a Marine lieutenant colonel and a national security adviser — from prosecution.

See the answer on the next page.

The post The Cynical Origin Of The Presidential Turkey Pardon appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Will Higher Sales Taxes Drive Shoppers Out Of Los Angeles?
articles.content:
The holiday shopping season is approaching, and unfortunately, increases in the cost of living due to inflation have made it harder for households to purchase holiday presents without exceeding their budgets. As a result, consumers are scrutinizing the prices they pay, including the sales taxes added to their purchases. One increasingly relevant question is whether it makes economic sense for Los Angeles residents to travel to neighboring cities to take advantage of lower sales tax rates.
Recently, Los Angeles voters approved Measure FD, which would increase the city’s sales tax rate by another 0.5 percentage points to help fund the Los Angeles Fire Department. This will increase the combined sales tax rate in Los Angeles is 10.75%. This rate is similar to other cities in the Los Angeles metropolitan area and has rates as high as 11.50%.
Compare this to neighboring Orange County, where some cities have considerably lower sales tax rates of 7.75%. This discrepancy is because these cities have little or no local sales taxes.
In the past, the sales tax rates for Los Angeles County and Orange County were almost equal. In 1990, the combined sales tax rate in Los Angeles was approximately 6.75% while most cities in Orange County were 6.25%.
A person who lives in Los Angeles might consider driving to Orange County and shopping where the sales tax rate is substantially lower. This is typically a tactic people done by people living close to a state with low or no sales taxes.
Would a difference of three percentage points in sales tax make a difference substantial enough to drive to another county? The answer depends on the amount being spent and the cost to travel there. Consider someone who plans to spend $500 on holiday presents. A three-percentage-point difference means $15 in tax savings. If the consumer spends $1,500, the savings increase to $45. These amounts are not insignificant, particularly for households operating on limited budgets.
However, the savings must be weighed against the cost of gasoline, vehicle wear and tear, and other transportation expenses. If the trip saves $15 in sales tax but costs $20 in gas, then the tax savings are meaningless. Also, the time spent traveling could be an inconvenience the consumer does not want to deal with.
California also has a use tax system designed to prevent consumers from avoiding sales taxes by purchasing merchandise in another city. When a consumer purchases merchandise in a city with a lower tax rate and subsequently uses that merchandise in a city with a higher tax rate, the consumer may owe additional use tax. The consumer will receive credit for tax already paid but must pay the difference. It should be noted that if the consumer purchases merchandise in a city with a higher tax rate and subsequently uses that merchandise in a city with a lower tax rate, the consumer will not get a tax refund.
Generally, the consumer reports the discrepancy and pays the sales tax through their income tax return by reporting use tax. But most consumers will not do this because they do not know about this reporting requirement, especially when shopping for everyday goods, some of which are sales tax exempt. Also, enforcement will be spotty or nonexistent because the tax deficiency is not large enough to warrant an audit.
Given the above, most people will not travel to another county to do a routine grocery run to avoid sales taxes because most groceries are sales tax exempt. But if the rate difference is high enough, some people may plan to purchase more expensive items in another county. More importantly, people could consider doing their Black Friday and holiday shopping elsewhere.
The gas expense argument may not be as strong these days as owners of electric vehicles generally spend far less by charging their cars at home.
If the consumer shift is strong enough, future sales tax increases can backfire. A higher tax rate may generate additional revenue from each taxable transaction, but that benefit could be offset if consumers do their shopping in neighboring cities. This could also impact local businesses because of lost sales.
As we enter the holiday shopping season, recent news of sales tax increases could have consumers thinking about whether they should shop in a more tax-friendly city. While consumers are required by law to repay the tax savings when they file their income tax returns, most will not do it because they do not know about this rule, and it will be inefficient to enforce it. A few percentage points may not seem particularly important on an individual purchase, but the difference becomes more noticeable when purchasing expensive electronics, appliances, clothing, and multiple holiday gifts. For consumers on fixed or limited budgets, every dollar matters.
Steven Chung is a tax attorney in Los Angeles, California. He helps people with basic tax planning and resolve tax disputes. He is also sympathetic to people with large student loans. He can be reached via email at stevenchungatl@gmail.com. Or you can connect with him on Twitter (@stevenchung) and connect with him on LinkedIn.
The post Will Higher Sales Taxes Drive Shoppers Out Of Los Angeles? appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Build Your Own Book, Own Your Own Career
articles.content:
In a recent conversation with John Cashman, President of Major, Lindsey & Africa, I explored what it really takes for lawyers to own their careers, from the decision to move firms to the book of business that makes a move possible.
In his appearance on the “Be That Lawyer” podcast, John brought the vantage point of someone who leads a top legal search firm and has seen thousands of lateral moves up close.
His message was candid: Great legal work matters, but a lawyer’s career is shaped just as much by client relationships, clear-eyed decisions, and an understanding of the business of law.
More Than Money
John’s answer about his “biggest mistake” was one every lawyer considering a move should hear.
As a young lawyer, he accepted an offer to join Winston & Strawn. His firm sweetened the pot with a counteroffer, and he stayed.
A year later, he was at Winston & Strawn anyway.
The ‘Cloudiness’ Problem
Law firms need to learn business leadership and operations if they want to attract the candidates they’re after.
Too often, the message to a recruit is that compensation will get figured out later, with no clear path laid out.
The ’95-5′ Differentiator — With Some Exceptions
While it’s much easier for a lawyer to move if they have a book of business, there are some exceptions.
And it isn’t only about the revenue.
Steve Fretzin is a five-time bestselling author, host of the BE THAT LAWYER and Future Rainmakers podcasts, and a business development coach who works exclusively with attorneys. For more than 18 years, he has helped lawyers build strong books of business without selling, pitching, or chasing, using his proven Sales-Free Selling™ approach. His clients consistently become top rainmakers and credit his coaching and systems for driving meaningful, measurable growth. Steve can be reached directly at steve@fretzin.com, or through his website at bethatlawyer.com. Connect with him on LinkedIn at https://www.linkedin.com/in/stevefretzin. His ALL NEW BE THAT LAWYER Community is changing how lawyers develop the skills never taught in law school. Learn more at bethatlawyer.com/community.
The post Build Your Own Book, Own Your Own Career appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Nothing Says Lovin’ Like Raises
articles.content:
Pillsbury has a new recipe for associate compensation. Well, half of one.
The firm told associates it “will continue to pay market level salaries to our on track associates and counsel in good standing” and adopted a new US salary scale effective January 1, 2027.
But when it comes to bonuses, there’s a little confusion over what the firm plans to do:
Let’s start with the good news, which is a match of the Milbank scale set over the summer:
|Class
|Salary
|1st Year Associates
|$235,000
|2nd Year Associates
|$245,000
|3rd Year Associates
|$270,000
|4th Year Associates
|$320,000
|5th Year Associates
|$385,000
|Senior Associate 1
|$410,000
|Senior Associate 2
|$440,000
|Counsel
|$455,000
Even though this scale has existed for months, Cravath rolled it out last week, so now everyone’s following that leader. Pillsbury will start paying the new salaries on January 1.
But Cravath’s memo wasn’t just a salary memo. Cravath also announced special bonuses ranging from $11,000 to $40,000 — upping the $6,000 to $25,000 Milbank paid over the summer. Pillsbury’s memo doesn’t mention special bonuses at all. After the table, associates get this sentence:
Our existing market based bonus and above market super bonus programs will remain in effect.
Pillsbury did match the market’s special bonuses last year, so maybe that’s the plan again. But in December 2024, when other firms were handing out specials, Pillsbury’s memo said, “Our existing market based bonus and above market Super Bonus programs also remain in effect.” Then came the twist. Rather than paying a special bonus, the firm bumped the Super Bonus 1 payout for fifth-years through counsel from $20,000 to $25,000. But the “Super Bonus 1” was only available for those hitting 2200 hours and up.
Now, the fair counterpoint. Pillsbury did come around last year. Its 2025 package was a four-column affair: base bonus, a standalone special bonus of $6,000 to $25,000, plus Super 1 ($20,000) and Super 2 ($30,000) on top. And that announcement came in December, separate from anything about salaries. So it’s entirely possible this is a salary memo, the bonus memo is still in the oven, and “market based bonus” is meant to swallow whatever the market now looks like.
Possible! But the firm doesn’t need to space out its memos — feel free to just deliver all the news at once.
If you’re at Pillsbury and hear more about bonuses, let us know.
The post Nothing Says Lovin’ Like Raises appeared first on Above the Law.
